patches.old: because C–F is the strongest bond and its electron-withdrawing inductive effect best stabilizes the anionic intermediate
patches.new: because the C–X bond is not broken in the rate-determining step — addition of the nucleophile is — so bond strength barely matters, while fluorine's strong inductive withdrawal makes that addition step fastest and best stabilizes the anionic intermediate
patches.reason: A strong C–F bond is a reason fluoride should be a *poor* leaving group, not a good one; stated as the cause it teaches the opposite of the mechanism. The actual explanation is that in SNAr the C–X bond breaks after the rate-determining addition, so leaving-group ability hardly affects the rate, and fluorine's electronegativity speeds the addition step (relative rate ~3300 vs iodide, with Cl, Br and I within a factor of about five of each other).

patches.old: Know the two-step mechanism cold: (1) electrophile generation, (2) rate-determining attack forming the arenium ion, (3) deprotonation restoring aromaticity.
patches.new: Know the sequence cold: (1) electrophile generation, then the two steps on the ring — (2) rate-determining attack forming the arenium ion and (3) deprotonation restoring aromaticity.
patches.reason: The sentence announced a two-step mechanism and then listed three steps. Only the attack and the deprotonation happen on the ring; electrophile generation precedes them.

patches.old: **Nonaromatic** compounds fail one or more criteria but are not cyclic, planar, and conjugated with 4n electrons.
patches.new: **Nonaromatic** compounds fail at least one of the four criteria and are not antiaromatic either — that is, they are not simultaneously cyclic, planar, fully conjugated and carrying 4n π electrons.
patches.reason: As written the sentence could be read as saying nonaromatic compounds are not cyclic, not planar and not conjugated, which is false — a nonaromatic ring may satisfy three of the four criteria. The distinction between nonaromatic and antiaromatic is directly tested.

visual.title: Why a substituent directs: where the arenium ion puts its charge
visual.alt: Three benzene rings show electrophilic attack at the ortho, meta and para positions relative to a substituent G. In each ring the three carbons that carry positive charge in the arenium ion are marked. For ortho and para attack the carbon bearing G is one of them; for meta attack it is not. Two panels below give the consequence: a lone-pair donor stabilises that contributor and so directs ortho and para, while a resonance withdrawer destabilises it, suppressing ortho and para and leaving meta.
visual.caption: The three charged carbons sit ortho and para to the carbon the electrophile hit. Whether the substituent's own carbon is one of them is the whole of the directing rule.
